content: If necessary, gently stimulate the baby to awaken them. Allow the baby to smell and lick the nipple, encouraging them to begin sucking. Express a small amount of breast milk into the baby’s mouth and wait for them to swallow before expressing more milk. When the baby has had enough, they will close their mouth and stop feeding. For very small babies, advise the mother to repeat this process every 1-2 hours, or every 2-3 hours for larger babies. Teach mothers how to heat-treat expressed breast milk. Carefully explain and demonstrate the process, then observe the mother practicing it. To heat-treat milk, express 50-150 ml of breast milk into a clean 450 ml glass jar, seal it with a lid, and label it with the baby’s name, date, and time. Place the jar in a pot containing boiling water (450 ml or 2 cm below the pot’s brim). If the jar floats, place a weight on top. Let it stand for 30 minutes. For alternative feeding methods, such as cup feeding expressed breast milk, teach the mother how to feed the baby using a cup. Do not feed the baby yourself. The baby will suck the milk and may spill some. Small babies will use their tongue to take milk into their mouth and swallow. The baby will stop feeding when they close their mouth or show no interest in taking more. If the baby does not consume the calculated amount, encourage longer or more frequent feeding sessions. If the mother cannot express enough milk initially or cannot breastfeed, consider donated heat-treated breast milk or formula as alternatives. Always use a cup for feeding if the mother is unavailable. Signs of adequate feeding include satisfaction after feeding, weight loss of less than 10% in the first week, a weight gain of at least 160 g per week after the first week, and frequent wet diapers corresponding to feeding frequency. Weigh the baby regularly to assess weight gain. For babies with normal birth weight and good breastfeeding, weigh monthly. For those on replacement feeding or isoniazid treatment, weigh every two weeks. For small or ill babies, weigh daily until they gain at least 15 g per day for three consecutive days. During the first month, acceptable weight changes include up to 10% loss in the first week, a gain of at least 160 g per week from weeks 2-4, and a minimum gain of 300 g by the end of the first month. Provide special breastfeeding support to mothers who are not yet breastfeeding due to illness or a baby’s inability to suckle. Teach the mother to express breast milk and use it to feed the baby by cup. If the baby has no mother, provide donated heat-treated breast milk or formula and teach the caregiver how to prepare and feed the baby. For mothers who are not breastfeeding, advise on relieving engorgement. Avoid breast stimulation, support the breasts with a well-fitting bra, and apply warm or cold compresses as preferred. Teach the mother to express just enough milk to relieve discomfort without stimulating increased production. Pain relief with ibuprofen or paracetamol may be used, and some women find plant-based remedies like raw cabbage leaves helpful. Advise seeking care if the breasts become painful, swollen, red, or if the mother feels unwell or has a fever above 38°C. Dry the baby immediately after birth and place them skin-to-skin on the mother’s abdomen or chest for at least two hours. If skin-to-skin contact is not possible, wrap the baby in warm, dry clothing and use a radiant warmer if necessary. Dress the baby in soft, clean clothes, cover their head with a cap, and keep them close to the mother. Assess the baby’s warmth every four hours by touching their feet. If cold, use skin-to-skin contact, add extra blankets, and reassess. At home, explain to the mother that babies need one more layer of clothing than adults and should sleep close to the mother to facilitate breastfeeding. For cord care, wash hands before and after handling the cord. Keep the stump clean and dry, folding the diaper below it. If soiled, wash with clean water and soap, then dry thoroughly. Do not apply substances or bandage the stump. Seek care if the umbilicus becomes red, drains pus, or bleeds. For hygiene, wash the baby’s face, neck, and underarms daily, and clean the buttocks when soiled. Bathe the baby only when necessary in a warm room with warm water, drying them thoroughly afterward. Avoid bathing babies under six hours old or if they are cold. If the baby is not breathing or gasping at birth, begin resuscitation within one minute. Keep the baby warm, position their head slightly extended, and suction only if the mouth or nose is full of secretions. If the baby still does not breathe, ventilate using a mask and bag, ensuring the chest rises. Assess the heart rate and breathing regularly. If the baby does not respond after 10 minutes of ventilation, stop and provide supportive care to the mother. Administer appropriate treatments and immunizations to the baby. Give 1 mg of vitamin K intramuscularly within one hour of birth. Provide antibiotics like ampicillin and gentamicin for serious infections. Teach the mother how to administer treatments at home, ensuring she understands the process. For HIV-exposed newborns, give antiretroviral drugs like nevirapine and zidovudine within 6-12 hours of birth and teach the mother how to continue treatment at home. Immunize the newborn with BCG, OPV-0, and hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth. Record the immunizations and advise the mother on when to return for the next dose. Follow up regularly to monitor the baby’s health and weight gain. Advise the mother to seek immediate care if the baby has difficulty breathing, convulsions, fever, bleeding, diarrhea, or is not feeding. For less urgent issues like feeding difficulties, eye pus, or skin pustules, visit a health center promptly.
